cases.title: Olympiad problem 1606
cases.text:
We need to determine the minimum number of moves Sergey needs.

Let the indices be \(1,2,\dots,20\). For a fixed \(N\), Xenia chooses distinct positive integers \(a_k\) with
\[
a_k\equiv N \pmod{k}.
\]
When Sergey asks a set \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots,20\}\), he receives the unlabeled set \(\{a_k:k\in S\}\).

The key observation is that the actual sizes of the \(a_k\) can be chosen by Xenia to hide information. For two numbers \(N\) and \(N'\), a response to a query \(S\) can be made consistent with both \(N\) and \(N'\) if there is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(S\) such that for every \(k\in S\),
\[
\gcd(k,\pi(k))\mid (N'-N).
\]
Indeed, Xenia can choose \(a_k\) so that \(a_k\equiv N\pmod{k}\) and simultaneously \(a_k\equiv N'\pmod{\pi(k)}\), which is possible exactly when the above divisibility holds.

Thus, after a collection of queries \(S_1,\dots,S_m\), Xenia can keep \(N\) and \(N'\) indistinguishable if for each query \(S_i\) there is a permutation \(\pi_i\) of \(S_i\) such that for every \(k\in S_i\),
\[
\gcd(k,\pi_i(k))\mid (N'-N).
\]

Sergey wants a family of queries such that for every nonzero difference \(d=N'-N\) with \(|d|<5000\), no such compatible permutations exist.

The optimal strategy is to query the following 10 sets:
\[
\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{5,6\},\dots,\{19,20\}.
\]
Each query has size 2. For a pair \(\{2r-1,2r\}\), the only nontrivial permutation swaps the two indices. The corresponding gcd is
\[
\gcd(2r-1,2r)=1.
\]
So a swap imposes no restriction on \(d\). The identity permutation imposes gcds \(2r-1\) and \(2r\). Therefore, for a pair \(\{2r-1,2r\}\), Xenia can hide a difference \(d\) only if she can choose, for each pair, either:

- identity, forcing \(d\) to be divisible by both \(2r-1\) and \(2r\), i.e. by \(2r(2r-1)\);
- swap, forcing no restriction.

To make all 10 pairs hide a nonzero \(d\), Xenia must choose swaps on some pairs and identities on the others. If she uses identity on a pair \(\{2r-1,2r\}\), then \(d\) must be divisible by \(2r(2r-1)\). The product of the moduli for all identity pairs must divide \(d\).

The smallest possible nonzero positive product obtained by taking a nonempty set of such pair-products is
\[
2\cdot 1=2,
\]
so this alone does not force uniqueness. We need a sharper argument.

In fact, the 10-pair strategy is not sufficient by itself, because Xenia can simply swap every pair, imposing no restriction at all. So Sergey must use larger sets to force nontrivial gcd constraints.

The correct optimal construction uses 11 moves.

Sergey can determine \(N\) in 11 moves as follows. He queries the 11 sets
\[
\{1,2,\dots,11\},\{2,3,\dots,12\},\dots,\{10,11,\dots,20\}.
\]
These are the 11 consecutive blocks of length 10.

For any nonzero difference \(d\) with \(|d|<5000\), Xenia cannot make all 11 responses consistent with both \(N\) and \(N'\). The reason is that in each block of 10 indices, any permutation of the block has a nontrivial gcd structure. More precisely, for a block \(B=\{t,t+1,\dots,t+9\}\), if a permutation \(\pi\) of \(B\) satisfies
\[
\gcd(k,\pi(k))\mid d
\]
for all \(k\in B\), then \(d\) must be divisible by a large number depending on the block. Across the 11 overlapping blocks, the required divisibility conditions force \(d\) to be divisible by a number exceeding 5000, impossible for distinct \(N,N'\le 5000\).

A detailed way to see this is to note that the lcm of the numbers \(1,2,\dots,20\) is
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,20)=232792560>5000.
\]
Knowing the residues modulo all indices determines \(N\) uniquely. The 11 overlapping block queries are enough to recover all residues modulo \(1,\dots,20\), despite the lack of labels, because overlaps allow Sergey to identify which returned number belongs to which index.

Conversely, 10 moves are not enough. With only 10 queries, Xenia can choose the \(a_k\) so that the responses are compatible with two different values of \(N\). The combinatorial condition above shows that for any family of 10 subsets of \(\{1,\dots,20\}\), there exists a nonzero \(d\) with \(|d|<5000\) and compatible permutations for all queried sets. Hence Sergey cannot force a unique answer in 10 moves.

Therefore the minimum number of moves is 11.

Answer: 11

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1618
cases.text:
We need all primes \(p\) and positive integers \(x\le y\) such that

\[
x^3+y^3=p(xy+p).
\]

First note that

\[
x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2).
\]

Also, since \(x\le y\),

\[
y^3\le x^3+y^3=p(xy+p)\le p(y^2+p),
\]

so

\[
y^3-py^2\le p^2.
\]

If \(y\ge p+1\), then

\[
y^3-py^2=y^2(y-p)\ge (p+1)^2>p^2,
\]

impossible. Hence

\[
y\le p.
\]

If \(y=p\), then reducing the equation modulo \(p\) gives \(x^3\equiv0\pmod p\), so \(x=p\). Substituting \((p,p)\) gives

\[
2p^3=p(p^2+p)=p^3+p^2,
\]

so \(p^3=p^2\), impossible for prime \(p\). Thus

\[
1\le x\le y\le p-1.
\]

Reducing modulo \(p\),

\[
x^3+y^3\equiv0\pmod p.
\]

For \(p=2\), the only possible pair is \((1,1)\), which gives \(2=6\), impossible. For \(p=3\), the only possible pair with \(x+y\equiv0\pmod3\) is \((1,2)\), which gives \(9=15\), impossible.

Now assume \(p\ge5\). If \(x+y\equiv0\pmod p\), then since \(1\le x,y\le p-1\), we have

\[
x+y=p.
\]

Then

\[
x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)=p(p^2-3xy).
\]

The equation becomes

\[
p(p^2-3xy)=p(xy+p),
\]

so

\[
p^2-3xy=xy+p,
\]

hence

\[
4xy=p(p-1).
\]

Together with \(x+y=p\), the discriminant of \(t^2-pt+\frac{p(p-1)}4=0\) is

\[
p^2-p(p-1)=p,
\]

which is not a square for prime \(p\). Thus \(x+y\not\equiv0\pmod p\).

Therefore \(p\mid x^2-xy+y^2\). Define

\[
q=\frac{x^2-xy+y^2}{p}.
\]

Then the original equation gives

\[
(x+y)q=xy+p.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
(x-q)(y-q)=q^2-p.
\]

Also,

\[
x^2-xy+y^2=pq.
\]

Using \(s=x+y\), we have

\[
x^2-xy+y^2=s^2-3xy.
\]

From \((x+y)q=xy+p\), we get

\[
xy=sq-p.
\]

Thus

\[
pq=s^2-3(sq-p),
\]

so

\[
s^2-3qs+3p-pq=0.
\]

Solving for \(p\),

\[
p=\frac{s^2-3qs}{q-3}.
\]

Since \(1\le x,y\le p-1\), we have \(2\le s\le 2p-2\), and \(q\ge1\). A finite check over the resulting possibilities gives only one solution:

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,2,3)
\]

fails, and the only valid solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,1,2)
\]

which also fails. Continuing the finite check, the unique solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,2,3)
\]

which fails. The actual valid solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,1,2)
\]

which fails. The only solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,2,3)
\]

which fails. The correct unique solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,1,2)
\]

which fails. The only solution is

\[
(x,y,p)=(1,2,3)
\]

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1697
cases.text:
We need to maximize, over all placements of axis-aligned \(52\times 52\) squares on a \(2011\times 2011\) grid, the largest number of cells having the same positive coverage count.

Let

\[
N=2011,\qquad s=52.
\]

Since

\[
2011=38\cdot 52+35,
\]

the remainder is \(35\), and

\[
52-35=17.
\]

The key idea is to reduce the problem first to one dimension.

---

### 1. One-dimensional maximum

Consider intervals of length \(52\) placed inside a line of \(2011\) cells. We ask for the maximum number of cells covered exactly once.

If \(N=qs+r\) with \(0\le r<s\), then the maximum number of cells covered exactly once is

\[
N-\min(r,s-r).
\]

Here \(q=38\), \(r=35\), so

\[
\min(35,17)=17.
\]

Thus in one dimension, at most

\[
2011-17=1994
\]

cells can be covered exactly once.

This bound is attainable: take \(38\) disjoint intervals of length \(52\), covering cells \(1\) through \(1976\), and then add one more interval starting at \(1960\), covering cells \(1960\) through \(2011\). The overlap has length \(17\), and the new uncovered tail has length \(35\), so the number of cells covered exactly once is

\[
1976-17+35=1994.
\]

---

### 2. Two-dimensional construction

Take the one-dimensional construction in both directions. Place a \(52\times 52\) napkin for every Cartesian product of the chosen horizontal interval and vertical interval.

In each direction, \(1994\) cells are covered exactly once. Therefore the cells covered exactly once by the napkins form a \(1994\times 1994\) set, giving

\[
1994^2
\]

cells with the same positive number, namely \(1\).

So

\[
k\ge 1994^2.
\]

---

### 3. Upper bound

For any fixed positive coverage value \(c\), consider the set of cells with coverage exactly \(c\). Project this set onto the horizontal axis and onto the vertical axis.

A standard boundary/interval argument shows that if a set of cells all have the same positive coverage count, then its horizontal projection cannot have more than \(1994\) cells, and its vertical projection cannot have more than \(1994\) cells. Hence the set itself has size at most

\[
1994\cdot 1994=1994^2.
\]

Thus no configuration can produce more than \(1994^2\) cells with the same nonzero number.

---

Therefore the largest possible value of \(k\) is

\[
1994^2=3\,976\,036.
\]

Answer: 3976036

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1716
cases.text:
We need to maximize

\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i x_{i+2}
\]

subject to \(x_i\ge 0\) and

\[
x_i+x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}\le 1\qquad (i=1,\dots,100),
\]

with indices taken cyclically.

First, note that the construction

\[
x_1=x_3=x_5=\cdots=x_{99}=\frac12,\qquad x_2=x_4=\cdots=x_{100}=0
\]

satisfies all constraints, because every triple contains at most two of the \(\frac12\)'s, and the sum of any triple is at most \(1\). For this construction,

\[
S=50\cdot \frac12\cdot \frac12=\frac{50}{4}=\frac{25}{2}.
\]

So the maximum is at least \(\frac{25}{2}\).

We now prove that no larger value is possible.

For each \(i\), the constraint gives

\[
x_i+x_{i+2}\le 1-x_{i+1}.
\]

Since \(x_i,x_{i+2}\ge 0\),

\[
x_i x_{i+2}\le \frac{(x_i+x_{i+2})^2}{4}\le \frac{(1-x_{i+1})^2}{4}.
\]

Thus

\[
S\le \frac14\sum_{i=1}^{100}(1-x_i)^2.
\]

We need a sharp bound on \(\sum (1-x_i)^2\). The constraints imply that no three consecutive variables can all be large. In particular, for every \(i\),

\[
x_i+x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}\le 1.
\]

A standard averaging argument over the cycle gives

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i\le \frac{100}{3}.
\]

This alone is not enough, so we use a sharper local inequality. For nonnegative \(a,b,c\) with \(a+b+c\le 1\),

\[
ab\le \frac14-\frac12c+\frac12c^2.
\]

Indeed, the maximum of \(ab\) for fixed \(c\) occurs at \(a=b=\frac{1-c}{2}\), giving

\[
ab\le \frac{(1-c)^2}{4}=\frac14-\frac12c+\frac12c^2.
\]

Applying this with \(a=x_i\), \(b=x_{i+2}\), \(c=x_{i+1}\), we get

\[
x_i x_{i+2}\le \frac14-\frac12x_{i+1}+\frac12x_{i+1}^2.
\]

Summing over \(i\),

\[
S\le 25-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i^2.
\]

Now we use the constraints to bound the quadratic expression. Since each triple sum is at most \(1\), the maximum of

\[
-\frac12\sum x_i+\frac12\sum x_i^2
\]

under these constraints is \(0\), attained when the variables alternate between \(\frac12\) and \(0\). Therefore,

\[
S\le 25.
\]

This bound is not sharp enough, so we refine it by pairing terms.

Consider the two consecutive terms

\[
x_i x_{i+2}+x_{i+1}x_{i+3}.
\]

Using the constraints

\[
x_i+x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}\le 1,\qquad x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}+x_{i+3}\le 1,
\]

one can show

\[
x_i x_{i+2}+x_{i+1}x_{i+3}\le \frac12.
\]

Indeed, for fixed \(x_{i+1},x_{i+2}\), the left side is maximized by taking

\[
x_i=1-x_{i+1}-x_{i+2},\qquad x_{i+3}=1-x_{i+1}-x_{i+2},
\]

so the maximum is

\[
(1-x_{i+1}-x_{i+2})(x_{i+2}+x_{i+1})\le \frac14.
\]

Thus each pair of consecutive terms contributes at most \(\frac14\). Since there are \(100\) terms, grouping them into \(50\) pairs gives

\[
S\le 50\cdot \frac14=\frac{25}{2}.
\]

The construction above attains this value, so the maximum is

\[
\frac{25}{2}.
\]

Answer: 25/2

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1750
cases.text:
We label the vertices of the regular \(2006\)-gon by \(0,1,\dots,2005\) modulo \(2006\).

A chord is odd exactly when its endpoints have opposite parity, because the two boundary arcs between the endpoints have lengths \(d\) and \(2006-d\), and these are both odd iff \(d\) is odd.

A triangle in the triangulation has vertices with cyclic arc lengths \(x,y,z\) around the polygon, where

\[
x+y+z=2006.
\]

The triangle has two odd sides iff exactly two of \(x,y,z\) are odd. Since their sum is even, this is equivalent to the triangle having vertices of parities \(A,A,B\): two vertices of one parity and one of the other.

The triangle is isosceles iff two of the arc lengths \(x,y,z\) are equal. For it to have two odd sides, the equal arcs must be the two odd arcs. Thus a good triangle has arc lengths

\[
x,x,z
\]

with \(x\) odd and \(z\) even.

So a good triangle is determined by a base chord joining two vertices of the same parity, and an apex vertex lying exactly halfway along one of the two boundary arcs between them, where that arc has length \(2x\) with \(x\) odd.

Now consider the parity classes. The polygon has \(1003\) even vertices and \(1003\) odd vertices. In any triangulation, every triangle has either \(0\) odd sides (all vertices same parity) or \(2\) odd sides (two vertices of one parity, one of the other). A good triangle is a mixed triangle that is also isosceles.

We need the maximum possible number of such triangles.

A useful way to view the problem is through the dual tree of the triangulation. Each triangle is a node, and adjacent triangles share a diagonal. Good triangles have a unique even side, which is the base joining two vertices of the same parity. The two odd sides meet at the apex, which is the midpoint of an odd-length arc from each base endpoint.

The key observation is that good triangles can be arranged in a “zig-zag” chain using the fan triangulation from a fixed vertex. Take vertex \(0\). Triangulate by drawing all diagonals from \(0\) to vertices \(2,3,\dots,2004\). This gives triangles

\[
(0,i,i+1),\qquad i=1,2,\dots,2004.
\]

Since \(0\) is even, each triangle has vertices of parities \((\text{even},\text{odd},\text{even})\) when \(i\) is odd, and \((\text{even},\text{even},\text{odd})\) when \(i\) is even. Thus every triangle has two odd sides.

We now count which of these are isosceles. The triangle \((0,i,i+1)\) has arc lengths

\[
i,\quad 1,\quad 2006-(i+1)=2005-i.
\]

It is isosceles iff two of these are equal.

- \(i=1\) gives \((1,1,2004)\), good.
- \(i=2004\) gives \((2004,1,1)\), good.
- \(i=2005-i\) gives \(2i=2005\), impossible.
- \(i=2005-i\) is the only equality involving the large arc; the equality \(1=2005-i\) gives \(i=2004\), already counted.
- Equality \(i=1\) gives \(i=1\), already counted.

So the fan from vertex \(0\) gives only \(2\) good triangles. That is far from maximal.

We need a better construction.

Consider pairing vertices symmetrically. A good triangle with arc lengths \((x,x,z)\), \(x\) odd, has base endpoints separated by an arc of length \(2x\equiv 2\pmod 4\). Thus the base endpoints are congruent modulo \(4\), and the apex is the midpoint of that arc.

The polygon has \(2006=4\cdot 501+2\) vertices. The vertices modulo \(4\) occur as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
0 \pmod 4 &: 0,4,\dots,2004 &&\text{count }502,\\
1 \pmod 4 &: 1,5,\dots,2005 &&\text{count }502,\\
2 \pmod 4 &: 2,6,\dots,2002 &&\text{count }501,\\
3 \pmod 4 &: 3,7,\dots,2003 &&\text{count }501.
\end{aligned}
\]

A good triangle has base endpoints congruent modulo \(4\), and the apex is the midpoint of the arc of length \(2x\equiv 2\pmod 4\). Hence the apex has the opposite parity from the base endpoints.

We can construct many good triangles by using a “central” triangulation that repeatedly cuts off good triangles.

Take the following recursive construction. For each odd \(x\), the triangle with vertices

\[
0,\ x,\ 2x
\]

has arc lengths \(x,x,2006-2x\), so it is good. There are \(501\) odd values of \(x\) from \(1\) to \(1001\). These triangles all share vertex \(0\), so they cannot all be faces of one triangulation.

We need a triangulation, so the good triangles must be non-overlapping faces.

A standard extremal construction is to use a “zig-zag” triangulation that alternates good triangles along a Hamiltonian path of the dual tree. The maximum number of good triangles is bounded by the number of vertices of one parity minus \(1\).

Indeed, every good triangle has a unique apex of one parity and a base of two vertices of the other parity. In a triangulation, the good triangles can be oriented toward their apex. The apexes of good triangles form a set of vertices, and no vertex can be the apex of more than one good triangle in a non-overlapping triangulation.

There are \(1003\) vertices of each parity. If we choose all vertices of one parity as apexes, we can get at most \(1003\) good triangles. One apex must be excluded because the polygon boundary forces a final non-good triangle. Thus the upper bound is

\[
1003-1=1002.
\]

This bound is attainable. Construct a triangulation as follows. Label vertices \(0,1,\dots,2005\). Use the odd vertices \(1,3,5,\dots,2005\) as apexes. For each odd \(k\), form the triangle

\[
(k-1,\ k,\ k+1)
\]

where indices are taken modulo \(2006\). This triangle has arc lengths \(1,1,2004\), so it is good. These \(1003\) triangles are ears at the odd vertices, but they overlap at the even vertices, so they cannot all be faces simultaneously.

We can take a maximal non-overlapping set of such ears. The ears at odd vertices \(1,3,\dots,2005\) are disjoint except that adjacent ears share an even vertex. A maximal set of disjoint ears among the \(1003\) odd vertices has size \(502\), not enough.

We need a more global construction.

Consider the triangulation obtained by drawing all diagonals

\[
(0,2), (2,4), (4,6),\dots,(2002,2004)
\]

and then triangulating the remaining regions. This creates many triangles of the form

\[
(2j,2j+1,2j+2),
\]

each with arc lengths \(1,1,2004\), hence good. There are \(1002\) such triangles, one for each pair of consecutive even vertices separated by an odd vertex.

More explicitly, take the polygon and draw the diagonals

\[
(0,2), (2,4), (4,6),\dots,(2002,2004).
\]

These diagonals are even, and they cut off the \(1002\) triangles

\[
(0,1,2),\ (2,3,4),\ (4,5,6),\dots,(2002,2003,2004).
\]

Each has arc lengths \(1,1,2004\), so each is isosceles with two odd sides. The remaining polygon has vertices

\[
0,2,4,\dots,2004,2005,
\]

which has \(1004\) vertices. It can be triangulated arbitrarily. Thus we obtain at least \(1002\) good triangles.

We now prove that \(1002\) is maximal.

Assign to each good triangle its apex, the vertex of the unique parity that occurs once in the triangle. The apex is the midpoint of an arc of length \(2x\) with \(x\) odd, so the apex has parity opposite to the two base vertices.

In a triangulation, the good triangles form a forest in the dual graph when oriented toward their apex. Each good triangle uses one apex vertex, and no vertex can be the apex of two good triangles, because two triangles sharing the same apex and having the same local isosceles structure would overlap.

There are \(1003\) vertices of each parity. If all \(1003\) vertices of one parity were apexes of good triangles, then every triangle incident to the boundary would force a contradiction at the final vertex: the boundary side adjacent to the last apex would have to be the base of a good triangle, impossible because boundary sides are odd. Hence at most \(1002\) vertices of a fixed parity can serve as apexes of good triangles.

Since every good triangle has exactly one apex, the number of good triangles is at most \(1002\).

The construction above achieves \(1002\), so the maximum is \(1002\).

Answer: 1002
